blocks.text: The drawingroom in Richard Rowan’s house at Merrion, a suburb of Dublin. On the right, forward, a fireplace, before which stands a low screen. Over the mantelpiece a giltframed glass. Further back in the right wall, folding doors leading to the parlour and kitchen. In the wall at the back to the right a small door leading to a study. Left of this a sideboard. On the wall above the sideboard a framed crayon drawing of a young man. More to the left double doors with glass panels leading out to the garden. In the wall at the left a window looking out on the road. Forward in the same wall a door leading to the hall and the upper part of the house. Between the window and door a lady’s davenport stands against the wall. Near it a wicker chair. In the centre of the room a round table. Chairs, upholstered in faded green plush, stand round the table. To the right, forward, a smaller table with a smoking service on it. Near it an easychair and a lounge. Coconut mats lie before the fireplace, beside the lounge and before the doors. The floor is of stained planking. The double doors at the back and the folding doors at the right have lace curtains, which are drawn halfway. The lower sash of the window is lifted and the window is hung with heavy green plush curtains. The blind is pulled down to the edge of the lifted lower sash. It is a warm afternoon in June and the room is filled with soft sunlight which is waning.
The mistress and Master Archie is at the bath. They never expected you. Did you send word you were back, Miss Justice?
Master Archie got your postcard with the views of Youghal. You’re tired out, I’m sure.
Don’t disturb him, Brigid. I can wait here till they come back if they are not long.
She crosses to the study door, opens it slightly and calls.
Rises and shakes hands, blushing slightly.
There is something in the letterbox, sir.
Takes a small bunch of keys from his pocket and hands them to her.
No, sir. Only them Italian newspapers.
Leave them on my desk, will you?
Please, sit down. Bertha will be back in a moment.
I had begun to think you would never come back. It is twelve days since you were here.
I thought of that too. But I have come.
Have you thought over what I told you when you were here last?
Do you think I have acted towards you﻿—badly? No? Or towards anyone?
Looks at him with a sad puzzled expression.
If I were a painter and told you I had a book of sketches of you you would not think it so strange, would you?
It is not quite the same case, is it?
Leans forward, resting his elbows on his knees, his hands joined.
Because it is written by me? Yes? Even if what you would find there is sometimes cruel?
Then it is my mind that attracts you? Is that it?
Hesitating, glances at him for an instant.

Why? Many reasons. To give Archie lessons. We have known one another so many years, from childhood, Robert, you and I﻿—haven’t we? You have always been interested in me, before I went away and while I was away. Then our letters to each other about my book. Now it is published. I am here again. Perhaps you feel that some new thing is gathering in my brain; perhaps you feel that you should know it. Is that the reason?
Otherwise I could not see you.
She looks at him for a moment and then turns aside quickly.
Have you confidence in me? Do you feel that you know me?
Hard to know me? I sent you from Rome the chapters of my book as I wrote them; and letters for nine long years. Well, eight years.
Yes, it was nearly a year before your first letter came.
On account of others or for want of courage﻿—which?
It was that that made me so reserved with you﻿—then﻿—even though I felt your interest in me, even though I felt that I too was something in your life.
Yet that separated me from you. I was a third person, I felt. Your names were always spoken together, Robert and Beatrice, as long as I can remember. It seemed to me, to everyone﻿ ﻿…
We are first cousins. It is not strange that we were often together.
He told me of your secret engagement with him. He had no secrets from me; I suppose you know that.
I always knew you would go some day. I did not suffer; only I was changed.
Everything was changed. His life, his mind, even, seemed to change after that.
It brought me near to death. It made me see things differently.
And so a coldness began between you, little by little. Is that it?
If there were convents in our religion perhaps there. At least, I think so at times.
You would try, yes. You were drawn to him as your mind was drawn towards mine. You held back from him. From me, too, in a different way. You cannot give yourself freely and wholly.
But do you feel that happiness is the best, the highest that we can know?
Leans back, his hands locked together behind his head.
Recovering himself, looks keenly at her for a moment.
Rises and walks nervously to and fro.
Did she write to you? I mean before﻿ ﻿…
While she lived she turned aside from me and from mine. That is certain.
From Bertha and from me and from our child. And so I waited for the end as you say; and it came.
Covers her face with her hands.
He presses his hand to his forehead.

She drove me away. On account of her I lived years in exile and poverty too, or near it. I never accepted the doles she sent me through the bank. I waited, too, not for her death but for some understanding of me, her own son, her own flesh and blood; that never came.
She raises her face and looks at him.
Holding out his hands to her.
Approaching, touches her lightly on the shoulder, and points to the crayon drawing on the wall.
He pauses for an instant and then goes on calmly.
Gazing again at the drawing, calmly, almost gaily.
A knock is heard at the hall door on the left.
Someone knocked. They have come back.
No, Bertha has a key. It is he. At least, I am going, whoever it is.
He goes out quickly on the left and comes back at once with his straw hat in his hand.
O, probably Robert. I am going out through the garden. I cannot see him now. Say I have gone to the post. Goodbye.
Coming towards her with outstretched hand which she takes.
O, they are lovely, sir. The mistress will be delighted with them.
Lays the roses carelessly on a chair out of sight.
Yes, sir. Sit down, sir. They’ll be here now any moment. The master was here.
She looks about her and with a half curtsey goes out on the right.
They were well when I left.
Yes, but I mean to say﻿ ﻿… O, well, you have arrived in your own characteristic way.
By Jove, Archie, too, is arriving in a characteristic way!
Smiles and holds out his hand.
Were you disappointed that I did not come last Friday for the lesson?
But now you must study, Archie.
Are you a good swimmer now?
Yes. I came to see him.
I’m sorry. If you had written or sent over word by the girl this morning﻿ ﻿…
But sit down, won’t you? You must be very tired.
I wouldn’t hear of such a thing, Miss Justice, after your long journey.
Going towards the door on the right.
He makes a movement to go.
O, very well. If that is it﻿ ﻿…
Did you not enjoy yourself down there, Miss Justice?
I go to see my father.
Well, afterwards you must stay to tea.
Coming towards him with the paper in her hand.
There is one word which I have never dared to say to you.
That I have a deep liking for you.
A short pause. The piano is heard faintly from the upper room.
Takes the bunch of roses from the chair.
She lays them on the table and unfolds the paper again.
I could not speak to you or follow you. There were too many people on the lawn. I wanted you to think over it and so I put it into your hand when you were going away.
Now you have dared to say it.
Moves his hand slowly past his eyes.
In that dress, with your slim body, walking with little even steps. I saw the moon passing in the dusk till you passed and left my sight.
Did you think of me last night?
I was awake half the night. I could hear your voice. I could see your face in the dark. Your eyes﻿ ﻿… I want to speak to you. Will you listen to me? May I speak?
I thought you were. You put away my poor flowers so quickly.
Takes them from the table and holds them close to her face.
Moving his chair closer to her.
Laying the flowers in her lap.
The other women. I hear you have so many admirers.
Do you speak to them in the same way?
She looks at him for a moment.
I have the right to call you by your name. From old times﻿—nine years ago. We were Bertha﻿—and Robert﻿—then. Can we not be so now, too?
Bertha, you knew. From the very night you landed on Kingstown pier. It all came back to me then. And you knew it. You saw it.
To two plain middleaged ladies, yes.
I recognized you at once. And I saw that you had got fat.
I think men speak like that to all women whom they like or admire. What do you want me to believe?
Yes, Robert. I think you too.
A little confused, tries to withdraw her hand.
He lifts her hand to his lips slowly. She rises suddenly and listens.
Did you hear the garden gate?
A short pause. The piano can be heard faintly from the upper room.
You want him to remain here.
For your sake because you are unhappy so far away. For his sake too because he should think of his future.
Do you not think he is strange?
You must not go away. I will not let you.
He kisses her eyes and then passes his hand over her hair.
He puts his arm around her.
He kisses her mouth and passes his hand many times over her hair.
Let me feel your lips touch mine.
And then you will be satisfied?
Closes her eyes and kisses him quickly.
Puts her hands on his shoulders.
O, don’t speak like that now, Robert.
Over, over. I want to end it and have done with it.
Listening to music and in the arms of the woman I love﻿—the sea, music and death.
Looks at him for a moment.
To my house. Not my mother’s over there. I will write the address for you. Will you come?
Tonight. Between eight and nine. Come. I will wait for you tonight. And every night. You will?
He kisses her with passion, holding her head between his hands. After a few instants she breaks from him. He sits down.
At the table, taking the roses.
I am afraid they are overblown.
Points to the chair near the little table on the right.
Passing his hand over his brow.
The room is rather dark, I think, with the blind down but if you wish﻿ ﻿…
Did he buy it or borrow it?
I shall smoke a cigarette. Thirtyseven copies have now been sold in Dublin.
He takes a cigarette from the box on the table, and lights it.
Conditions? You mean about the future?
Writing one of your leading articles, in fact.
Of course, it is your affair, Richard. However, you are not so young now as you were then. The expression is quite in the style of my leading articles, isn’t it?
Do you, or do you not, want me to give the lie to my past life?

I am thinking of your future life﻿—here. I understand your pride and your sense of liberty. I understand their point of view also. However, there is a way out; it is simply this. Refrain from contradicting any rumours you may hear concerning what happened﻿ ﻿… or did not happen after you went away. Leave the rest to me.
You will set these rumours afloat?
For the sake of something else too﻿—our friendship, our lifelong friendship.
Not only for your sake. Also for the sake of﻿—your present partner in life.
He crushes his cigarette softly on the ashtray and then leans forward, rubbing his hands slowly.
All things come to those who wait.
Sits down again, leaning back on the lounge.
He lifts his glass and drinks.
For me it is quite natural to kiss a woman whom I like. Why not? She is beautiful for me.
He takes up a flat stone which lies on the table.
He places it against his lips.
It is an act of union between man and woman. Even if we are often led to desire through the sense of beauty can you say that the beautiful is what we desire?
Pressing the stone to his forehead.
Turning over the stone, he presses the other side to his forehead.
Yes. I suppose they do.﻿ ﻿… This beautiful cool stone does me good. Is it a paperweight or a cure for headache?
Bertha brought it home one day from the strand. She, too, says that it is beautiful.
He raises his glass and drinks. A pause.
Is that all you wanted to say to me?

Eight. But, like yourself, he is free and easy about time. Now, Richard, you must go there. That is all. I feel tonight will be the turningpoint in your life. You will live here and work here and think here and be honoured here﻿—among our people.
He folds his arms across his chest.
he unfolds his arms and extends his right arm, averting his head
In my time the dunghill was so high.
The second one for me, please.
He drinks and goes on as before.
Sits up suddenly and leans his elbows on the table.
Lights and offers him a match.
The faith of a master in the disciple who will betray him.
He turns and says in a friendly tone.
One more match and I am happy.
Congratulate me, Beatty. I have won over Richard.
Crossing to the door on the right, calls.
On what are you to be congratulated?
I am not a descendant of Hamilton Rowan.
Thanks. But do not believe him.
Wait, Beatty. I shall accompany you.
I want to ask you a thing.
Sitting on the end of the lounge, stares in front of him.
Will you ask mamma to let me go out in the morning with the milkman?
Yes. In the milkcar. He says he will let me drive when we get on to the roads where there are no people. The horse is a very good beast. Can I go?
Ask mamma now can I go. Will you?
He said he will show me the cows he has in the field. Do you know how many cows he has?
Eleven. Eight red and three white. But one is sick now. No, not sick. But it fell.
While you have a thing it can be taken from you.
He bends his head and presses his son’s hand against his cheek.
How could a robber rob a cow? Everyone would see him. In the night, perhaps.
Are there robbers here like in Rome?
No, sit there, pappie. You wait and ask her when she comes back. I won’t be here. I’ll be in the garden.
Leans his chin in his hand.
Yes. I asked him what it meant.
What did he say it meant?
He said I must know. I said I had an idea. Then he told me he liked me very much. That I was beautiful﻿—and all that.
Since when did he say he liked you?
He was very nervous. You saw that?
Yes. I saw it. What else went on?
He asked me to give him my hand.
Then he asked could he embrace me﻿—even once?﻿ ﻿… And then﻿ ﻿…
He put his arm round me.
Stares at the floor for a moment, then looks at her again.
Did he ask you to kiss him?
Hesitates, then looking straight at him.
Excited? Yes, I think he was. He sighed. He was dreadfully nervous.
Resting his forehead on his hand.
Crosses towards the lounge and stands near him.
I am not. Jealous of what?
Yes, that’s all. Except that he asked me would I meet him.
No, a house he has. He wrote the address for me.
She goes to the desk, takes the key from the flower vase, unlocks the drawer and returns to him with the slip of paper.
He throws the slip on the couch and rises suddenly.
Walks away from her a few paces and stands still, thinking, holding his chin.
He told me to take the tram at Lansdowne Road and to ask the man to let me down there. Is it﻿ ﻿… is it a bad place?
He returns to the lounge and sits down.
No answer. He said he would wait.
Every night, he said. Between eight and nine.
Did he ask you had I any suspicion?
He halts, thrusting his hands into his pockets.
Flings the slip on the couch.
I never tried to do such a thing, Bertha. You know I cannot be severe with a child.
Because you never loved your own mother. A mother is always a mother, no matter what. I never heard of any human being that did not love the mother that brought him into the world, except you.

Who taught him to be? Who taught him to run to meet you? Who told him you would bring him home toys when you were out on your rambles in the rain, forgetting all about him﻿—and me? I did. I taught him to love you.
Yes, dear. I know it was you.
To have complete liberty with﻿—that girl.
You did. I thought it was a kind of friendship between you﻿—till we came back, and then I saw.
Believe me, Bertha dear. Believe me as I believe you.
Throws out his hands with a sigh and moves away from her.

But I care. What would he say if he knew? You, who talk so much of the high kind of feeling you have for me, expressing yourself in that way to another woman. If he did it, or other men, I could understand because they are false pretenders. But you, Dick! Why do you not tell him then?
He doesn’t say one thing and do another. He is honest in his own way.
Plucks one of the roses and throws it at her feet.

You may make fun of him as much as you like. I understand more than you think about that business. And so will he. Writing those long letters to her for years, and she to you. For years. But since I came back I understand it﻿—well.
You do not. Nor would he.
Comes nearer; in a calmer tone.

I do. But I believe you will get very little from her in return﻿—or from any of her clan. Remember my words, Dick. Because she is not generous and they are not generous. Is it all wrong what I am saying? Is it?
The tea is on the table, ma’am.
Is Master Archie in the garden?
Am I to go to this place?
I want to find out what he means. Am I to go?
Why do you ask me? Decide yourself.
Do you tell me to go?
Do you forbid me to go?
Tell me not to go and I will not.
In the morning? She said yes?
He puts his arm round his son’s shoulders and looks down at him fondly.

A room in Robert Hand’s cottage at Ranelagh. On the right, forward, a small black piano, on the rest of which is an open piece of music. Farther back a door leading to the street door. In the wall, at the back, folding doors, draped with dark curtains, leading to a bedroom. Near the piano a large table, on which is a tall oil lamp with a wide yellow shade. Chairs, upholstered, near this table. A small cardtable more forward. Against the back wall a bookcase. In the left wall, back, a window looking out into the garden, and, forward, a door and porch, also leading to the garden. Easychairs here and there. Plants in the porch and near the draped folding doors. On the walls are many framed black and white designs. In the right corner, back, a sideboard; and in the centre of the room, left of the table, a group consisting of a standing Turkish pipe, a low oil stove, which is not lit, and a rocking-chair. It is the evening of the same day.
First of all let me put these outside.
He takes the hat and umbrella, leaves them in the hall and returns.
Is about to look again at his watch; then stops.
Passes his hand over his forehead.
I know everything. I have known for some time.
Since it began between you and her.
Explain to me what is the word you longed and never dared to say to her. If you can or will.
Looks down, then raises his head.
Then why did you wish to keep secret your wooing?
With a nervous movement of the hands.
No. Time after time, as it happened.
Passes his hand again over his forehead.
Even if Bertha had not told me I should have known. Did you not see that when I came in this afternoon I went into my study suddenly for a moment?
To give you time to recover yourself. It made me sad to see your eyes. And the roses too. I cannot say why. A great mass of overblown roses.
That was why I did not hate you. The whole thing made me sad all at once.
He stares before him for some moments in silence, as if dazed; then, without turning his head, continues.
And she, too, was trying me; making an experiment with me for your sake!
You know women better than I do. She says she felt pity for you.
Like all men you have a foolish wandering heart.
They look at each other for some moments in silence.
You forget that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence: and the kingdom of heaven is like a woman.
For what you have done for her? So much! You claim nothing?
After a pause strikes his forehead with his hand.
But if you love﻿ ﻿… What else is it?
If you had it and I could feel that you had it﻿—even now﻿ ﻿…
With a little gesture of despair.
You spoke of conscience﻿ ﻿… Did he seem to you a child only﻿—or an angel?
Never then? Never even﻿ ﻿… with her? Tell me. I wish to know.

I feel in my heart something different. I believe that on the last day (if it ever comes), when we are all assembled together, that the Almighty will speak to us like this. We will say that we lived chastely with one other creature﻿ ﻿…

Or that we tried to. And He will say to us: Fools! Who told you that you were to give yourselves to one being only? You were made to give yourselves to many freely. I wrote that law with My finger on your hearts.
Yes. Can we close our heart against an affection which we feel deeply? Should we close it? Should she?
We are speaking of bodily union.
Affection between man and woman must come to that. We think too much of it because our minds are warped. For us today it is of no more consequence than any other form of contact﻿—than a kiss.
If it is of no consequence why are you dissatisfied till you reach that end? Why were you waiting here tonight?
Passion tends to go as far as it can; but, you may believe me or not, I had not that in my mind﻿—to reach that end.
Reach it if you can. I will use no arm against you that the world puts in my hand. If the law which God’s finger has written on our hearts is the law you say I too am God’s creature.
I always felt it. In myself and in others.
Because I knew a woman who seemed to me to be doing that﻿—carrying out that idea in her own life. She interested me very much.
O, not lately. When you were away.
You see, I am more honest than you thought.
I wish you had not thought of her now﻿—whoever she was, or is.
Moving his chair a little closer.
O, Richard, why did you do that?
No. But tell her, waken her from sleep to tell her. It was piercing her heart.
She must know me as I am.
But that is not you as you are. A moment of weakness.
I tried to give her a new life.
And you have. A new and rich life.
Is it worth what I have taken from her﻿—her girlhood, her laughter, her young beauty, the hopes in her young heart?

And that other law of nature, as you call it: change. How will it be when you turn against her and against me; when her beauty, or what seems so to you now, wearies you and my affection for you seems false and odious?
And you turn even against yourself for having known me or trafficked with us both?
Lays his hand on his arm.
He breaks off and turns aside, unable to speak.
Look here, Richard. We have said all there is to be said. Let the past be past.
He turns half round towards him.
I know. And it was noble of you.
Looks up at him with a steady gaze.
Looks away again: in a lower voice.
To be forever a shameful creature and to build up my soul again out of the ruins of its shame.
And that is why you wished that she﻿ ﻿…
From pride and from ignoble longing. And from a motive deeper still.
He returns to his place and begins to speak at once, drawing his chair closer.

May it not be that we are here and now in the presence of a moment which will free us both﻿—me as well as you﻿—from the last bonds of what is called morality. My friendship for you has laid bonds on me.
I acted in the dark, secretly. I will do so no longer. Have you the courage to allow me to act freely?
Passes his hand across his brow.
A knock is heard at the hall door.
Because you are generous enough to allow me?
Angry or not, I will not live on your generosity. You have asked her to meet you here tonight and alone. Solve the question between you.
I shall go. I tell you. Wait out there if you wish.
Yes, it is. How did you find it?
Did you think I would not?
I knew you could not remain away. You see, after all you are like all other men. You had to come. You are jealous like the others.
You seem annoyed to find me here.
I told him I knew everything, that I had known for a long time. He asked how. I said from you.
I cannot read in his heart.
I told him you were sincere with him.
He does not believe it. Nobody would believe it. I should have told him first﻿—not you.
I thought he was a common robber, prepared to use even violence against you. I had to protect you from that.
That I could have done myself.
It would have been enough to have told him that you knew I was here. Now I can find out nothing. He hates me. He is right to hate me. I have treated him badly, shamefully.
Gazes into her eyes and then lets her hand fall.
With a slight toss of her head.
Naturally. My part is ended here.
Her ladyship. I suppose it is all planned so that you may have a good opportunity. To meet her and have an intellectual conversation!
With an outburst of rude anger.
Unpins her hat and sits down.
Then you have come here and led him on in this way on account of me. Is that how it is?
There is one person in all this who is not a fool. And that is you. I am though. And he is.

He has. Of all the persons I met since I came back he is the only one who has. And he knows what they only suspect. And that is why I liked him from the first and like him still. Great respect for me she has! Why did you not ask her to come away with you nine years ago?
You know why, Bertha. Ask yourself.
Yes, I know why. You knew the answer you would get. That is why.
That is not why. I did not even ask you.
Yes. You knew I would go, asked or not. I do things. But if I do one thing I can do two things. As I have the name I can have the gains.
I am not. Only I feel for him, too.

And I do too. You may be his and mine. I will trust you, Bertha, and him too. I must. I cannot hate him since his arms have been around you. You have drawn us near together. There is something wiser than wisdom in your heart. Who am I that I should call myself master of your heart or of any woman’s? Bertha, love him, be his, give yourself to him if you desire﻿—or if you can.
At the same time she retreats towards the middle of the room. Then she calls again in the same way.
Catching sight of him, starts back: then, quickly.
Looking towards the door on the right.
With a movement of his head.
She comes to the table and rests her hand on the corner.
Clasping his hands at his back, quietly but a little defiantly.
Comes forward a few steps, halts: then impulsively:
And would you have told me?
Try to understand me, Robert. You must try.
Why do you stand like that near the door? It makes me nervous to look at you.
I am trying to understand. And then I am afraid.
Distressed, lays her hand on his arm.
She passes her hands over his coat.
But you are really drenched. You must change your coat.
Please change your coat, Robert, when I ask you. You might get a very bad cold from that. Do, please.
Points to the door at the back.
Well, go in and take that off.
I will wait here for you.
He goes quickly towards the bedroom door; then turns round.
No, I will wait. But don’t be long.
I am in the dark here. I must light the lamp.
Can you admire it from where you are?
Come here, quickly! Quickly, I say!
He appears in the doorway, wearing a darkgreen velvet jacket. Seeing her agitation, he comes quickly towards her.
Promise me, Robert, not to think of such a thing. Never. If you like me at all. I thought that moment﻿ ﻿…
But promise me if you like me.
If I like you, Bertha! I promise. Of course, I promise. You are trembling all over.
Let me sit down somewhere. It will pass in a moment.
My poor Bertha! Sit down. Come.
He leads her towards a chair near the table. She sits down. He stands beside her.
Yes. It was only for a moment. I was very silly. I was afraid that﻿ ﻿… I wanted to see you near me.
That﻿ ﻿… that you made me promise not to think of?
Now you are here. I can see you. Now it has passed.
Yes, because it annoyed me that you could think I was like﻿ ﻿… like the other women I suppose you knew that way. I think that Dick is right too. Why should there be secrets?
You know the kind he is. He asks about everything. The ins and outs.
Of course. I told him all.
And how did he take it? Tell me. I want to know everything, too.
No, Robert. Why should I be?
He points vaguely here and there.
Touching his jacket with her fingers.
Also. I will keep no secrets from you.
You remind me of someone in a picture. I like you in it﻿ ﻿… But you are not angry, are you?
He walks away from her a few paces. A gust of wind makes the lamp on the table flicker. He lowers the wick slightly.
Did he tell you that about himself?
Yes. He told me. We all confess to one another here. Turn about.
Not now. Only I dislike to think of it.
It is merely something brutal, you think? Of little importance?
Looking at her over his shoulder.
I said in myself. But would you?
You think I would revenge myself? Is Dick not to be free too?
Gazing at him with wide open eyes.
Stretches out both hands to her.
He crosses before the table rapidly and sits down beside her.
Turning towards him, places her left hand on his shoulder.
A gust of wind enters through the porch, with a sound of moving leaves. The lamp flickers quickly.
Without rising, he bends towards the table, and turns down the wick more. The room is half dark. The light comes in more strongly through the doorway of the bedroom.
The wind is rising. I will close that door.
Yes, when you slighted the common simple gift I had to offer you﻿—and took his gift instead.
No. Because you had chosen him. I saw that. I saw it on the first night we met, we three together. Why did you choose him?
And when you and he went away for your walk and I went along the street alone I felt it. And when he spoke to me about you and told me he was going away﻿—then most of all.
Because it was then that I was guilty of my first treason towards him.
Robert, what are you saying? Your first treason against Dick?
Raising her head and looking at him.
Well, Robert. It was unkind of you towards me. But I forgive you because you were thinking of his happiness and mine.
Nor I you. I knew I would see you again. I knew it the night you went away﻿—that you would come back. And that was why I wrote and worked to see you again﻿—here.
And here I am. You were right.
Lowering his voice and bending nearer to her.
Looks round the room, without answering.
He knows we like each other. Is there any harm, then?
Moves closer to her and presses her arm as he speaks.
Puts his arm about her shoulder.

The rain falling. Summer rain on the earth. Night rain. The darkness and warmth and flood of passion. Tonight the earth is loved﻿—loved and possessed. Her lover’s arms around her; and she is silent. Speak, dearest!
Suddenly leans forward and listens intently.
A gust of wind blows in through the porch, with a sound of shaken leaves. The flame of the lamp leaps.
Only the wind. We have light enough from the other room.
He stretches his hand across the table and puts out the lamp. The light from the doorway of the bedroom crosses the place where they sit. The room is quite dark.
I am going now, Robert. It is very late. Be satisfied.
She does not answer. In the silence the rain is heard falling.

The drawingroom of Richard Rowan’s house at Merrion. The folding doors at the right are closed and also the double doors leading to the garden. The green plush curtains are drawn across the window on the left. The room is half dark. It is early in the morning of the next day. Bertha sits beside the window looking out between the curtains. She wears a loose saffron dressing gown. Her hair is combed loosely over the ears and knotted at the neck. Her hands are folded in her lap. Her face is pale and drawn.
Merciful hour, ma’am. You put the heart across me. Why did you get up so early?
After seven, ma’am. Are you long up?
I didn’t sleep all night. So I got up to see the sun rise.
She goes to the door of the study and knocks.
Out there, on the strand, is it?
Comes towards her and leans over the back of a chair.
No, Brigid, that time comes only once in a lifetime. The rest of life is good for nothing except to remember that time.
Is silent for a moment: then says kindly.
Yes, I would. But the milkman has not come yet.
No. Master Archie told me to wake him before he came. He’s going out for a jaunt in the car. But I’ve a cup left overnight. I’ll have the kettle boiling in a jiffy. Would you like a nice egg with it?
Or a nice bit of toast?
No, Brigid, thanks. Just a cup of tea.
She stops, turns back and goes towards the door on the left.
Comes to her and, putting up his face to be kissed, says:
I said you were to put it on, didn’t I?
Takes a comb from her head and combs his hair back at both sides.
He went to bed immediately after you went out last night, ma’am.
You know he’s going to let me drive, mamma.
Replacing the comb in her hair, embraces him suddenly.
Well, he’s daft on horses, anyhow.
He makes the gesture of cracking a whip and shouts at the top of his voice.
Beat the poor horse, is it?
She takes her handkerchief from the pocket of her gown, wets it with her tongue and cleans his mouth.
The noise is heard of a milkcan rattled on the railings before the window.
Draws aside the curtains and looks out.
He kisses her hastily and turns to go.
Mind yourself, Archie, and don’t be long or I won’t let you go any more.
All right. Look out of the window and you’ll see me. Goodbye.
Look at the sit of him! As serious as you like.
She listens. A knock is heard at the hall door.
Stands a moment in doubt, then.
Sits opposite her, pointing to her paper.
Yes. Here it is. A long article, a leading article, by my cousin. All his life is here. Do you wish to see it?
Takes the paper, and opens it.
Is it﻿ ﻿… for Dick or against him?
Yes. Very late. I heard him come home. It was long after two.
How quick you were to think of that!
Crumples together the paper in her hands, breathlessly.
Sinking back, with a forced laugh.
Only the noise of his valise being pulled along the floor. Then I heard him walking about his room, whistling softly. And then locking it and strapping it.
But why should they quarrel? Have you noticed anything between them?
I thought I did. A coldness.
Yes. I bought the paper at once to see. But why, then, is he going away so suddenly? I feel that there is something wrong. I feel that something has happened between them.
Yes, you. By your letters to him and then by speaking to your cousin as you said just now. Do you not think that you are the person who brought him back?
Watches her for a moment; then turning aside.
Study or bedroom. You may call it what you please. He sleeps there, too, on a sofa. He slept there last night. I can show you if you don’t believe me.
You could know it just as well. You are very intimate in this house.
I am not the only person who is intimate here.
Why should I hate you? I have never hated anyone.
Can you say that to me﻿—truly? Look at me.
You said just now that another person is intimate in this house. You meant your cousin﻿ ﻿… Was it he?
She stands up suddenly and goes towards the davenport.
She takes a writing pad from the drawer and writes a few lines in great haste.
She goes out by the door on the left rapidly.
Stands in the doorway, observing her for some moments.
he points out towards the strand
Otherwise I could not see you,
Advancing towards her, holding out his hand.
Suddenly takes off her spectacles and places the paper in his hands.
Death of the Very Reverend Canon Mulhall
He begins to read in a rather loud hard voice.
those who left her in her hour of need
She stands up and walks excitedly to and fro.
I gave it to himself, ma’am.
He was just going out, ma’am. He told me to say he’d be here after me.
She goes out on the left.
I will see you to the gate.
You have not spoken to me.
I have nothing to say. Have you?
Do you not wish to know﻿—about what happened last night?
I will tell you if you ask me.
You will tell me. But I will never know. Never in this world.
Clenching his hands in the air, passionately.
Why, then, did you leave me last night?
I did not make myself. I am what I am.
Listen to you! She is the person for listening. Why would you waste your time with me? Talk to her.
So that you could meet your lover﻿—freely?
Gazing before her and speaking with intense passion.
Holding out her arms before her.
Pushes his hand aside and starts to her feet.
Closing the door quietly behind him.
Advancing towards the table on which the paper lies, glances at it.
When did you write it? Last night﻿—after I went away?
And you could write last night!
He lays his hat on the table and takes her hand.
To foreign parts. That is, to my cousin Jack Justice, alias Doggy Justice, in Surrey. He has a nice country place there and the air is mild.
Yes. It is not pleasant for me to remain here just now.
But, Robert, you must speak to him.
What am I to say to him?
He will believe that you are going away because you are afraid to face him after last night.
He gazes earnestly into her eyes.
And that is the truth﻿—a dream? That is what I am to tell?
There is no answer. She beats her hand loudly on the panel of the door and calls in an alarmed voice.
There is nothing to thank me for, Richard. Now and always I am your friend. Now more than ever before. Do you believe me, Richard?
Fresh Dublin bay herrings! Fresh Dublin bay herrings! Dublin bay herrings!
Raises his face and leans back to listen.
I failed, Richard. That is the truth. Do you believe me?
I failed. She is yours, as she was nine years ago, when you met her first.
When we met her first, you mean.
He looks down for some moments.

She went away. I was left alone﻿—for the second time. I went to the vicechancellor’s house and dined. I said you were ill and would come another night. I made epigrams new and old﻿—that one about the statues also. I drank claret cup. I went to my office and wrote my article. Then﻿ ﻿…
Then I went to a certain nightclub. There were men there﻿—and also women. At least, they looked like women. I danced with one of them. She asked me to see her home. Shall I go on?
I saw her home in a cab. She lives near Donnybrook. In the cab took place what the subtle Duns Scotus calls a death of the spirit. Shall I go on?

She wept. She told me she was the divorced wife of a barrister. I offered her a sovereign as she told me she was short of money. She would not take it and wept very much. Then she drank some melissa water from a little bottle which she had in her satchel. I saw her enter her house. Then I walked home. In my room I found that my coat was all stained with the melissa water. I had no luck even with my coats yesterday: that was the second one. The idea came to me then to change my suit and go away by the morning boat. I packed my valise and went to bed. I am going away by the next train to my cousin, Jack Justice, in Surrey. Perhaps for a fortnight. Perhaps longer. Are you disgusted?
Why did you not go by the boat?
You intended to go without saying goodbye﻿—without coming here?
My story is not very nice, is it?
Bertha sent me a message to come.
But for that I should not have come.
Did it strike you that if you had gone without coming here I should have understood it﻿—in my own way?
What, then, do you wish me to believe?
I wish you to believe that I failed. That Bertha is yours now as she was nine years ago, when you﻿—when we﻿—met her first.
Do you want to know what I did?
Hearing voices about me. The voices of those who say they love me.
Points to the door on the right.
Smiles and touches his forehead with his right forefinger.
A queer way of showing their love, I must say! And will you despair?
Open the window! Open the window!
Open the window, please, will you?
Perhaps, there, Richard, is the freedom we seek﻿—you in one way, I in another. In him and not in us. Perhaps﻿ ﻿…
And where were you, my young gentleman?
He takes off his cap and throws it on a chair.
Takes his hat from the table.
A fairy story? Why not? I am your fairy godfather.
Dick, dear, do you believe now that I have been true to you? Last night and always?
You left me: and I waited for you to come back to me. Dick, dear, come here to me. Sit down. How tired you must be!
She draws him towards the lounge. He sits down, almost reclining, resting on his arm. She sits on the mat before the lounge, holding his hand.
Yes, dear. I waited for you. Heavens, what I suffered then﻿—when we lived in Rome! Do you remember the terrace of our house?
Caressing her cheek with his hand.
And I used to look at the sky, so beautiful, without a cloud and the city you said was so old: and then I used to think of Ireland and about ourselves.
Yes. Ourselves. Not a day passes that I do not see ourselves, you and me, as we were when we met first. Every day of my life I see that. Was I not true to you all that time?
Wherever you go, I will follow you. If you wish to go away now I will go with you.
I will remain. It is too soon yet to despair.
How wounded, dear? Explain to me what you mean. I will try to understand everything you say. In what way are you wounded?
Releases his hand and, taking her head between his hands, bends it back and gazes long into her eyes.
Still gazing at her and speaking as if to an absent person.
Forget me, Dick. Forget me and love me again as you did the first time. I want my lover. To meet him, to go to him, to give myself to him. You, Dick. O, my strange wild lover, come back to me again!
